title: Start simple: A one-page design document for your first game
summary: A beginner’s guide to scoping your first game: set limits, cut features, and plan the whole thing with our free one-page game design document template.
body_markdown:
## How to set the scope for your first game in four steps


### 1. Describe what the player does in one sentence.


Start with a single, specific sentence that explains what playing your game actually is. Focus on what the player does and directly controls, not how it feels. For example: “The player steers a spaceship to collect points while avoiding obstacles.” This is called the[core game loop](https://unity.com/blog/find-your-core-game-loop) .


This sentence is your core concept. Everything else in your plan should support it. (If you’re not sure what the player does over and over, start with our guide to finding your core game loop.)


### 2. List only what must exist for that sentence to work.


Now write down every feature that absolutely has to exist for someone to play the game the way you described. For the spaceship example, the player needs to be able to move the ship, collect points, and take damage when they hit an obstacle.


Anything that doesn’t directly support the core idea gets left out, at least for now. That’s your minimum version of the game: the smallest thing that’s still playable.


### 3. Sort everything else into four buckets.


You’ll still have a list of ideas you love. Don’t delete them – sort them. A simple method from project planning (MoSCoW) uses four labels:


- **Must have:** The game doesn’t work without it.
- **Should have:** Important, but the game still works without it.
- **Could have:** Nice to have, with less impact if it’s left out.
- **Won’t have this time:** Not in this version.


To test whether something is really a must-have, ask: “What happens if this is missing?” If the honest answer is “the game doesn’t work,” it’s a must-have. If there’s any way around it, it isn’t. Some planners even suggest starting with everything in the “won’t have” bucket and making each idea earn its way out.


Writing down your won’t-haves is just as useful as writing down your must-haves. It makes the edges of your project clear and stops cut ideas from quietly sneaking back in later.


### 4. Decide what “done” looks like for your game.


A game without a finish line never ends. Before you start, write down what “finished” means for this version. A simple checklist might include:


- A title screen
- Your core gameplay loop
- A way to win or lose
- Sound effects
- A score or a way to track progress
- A playable version you can share


When every box is checked, you’re done. Anything else is a bonus or the start of version two.
